subject: Banking
title: Overend Gurney: Victorian Bank Run
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Overend Gurney: Victorian Bank Run.

hook.text: Overend Gurney was London's biggest discount bank. On May 10, 1866.

buildup.text: The bank had lent recklessly to railway speculators and shipbuilders. When loans went bad, losses exceeded capital.

discovery.text: Depositors rushed to withdraw. The Bank of England refused to bail them out.

twist.text: This crisis established the lender of last resort principle.

climax.text: One bank's failure reshaped central banking. Overend Gurney's collapse created the modern lender of last resort concept.

punchline.text: The Bank of England refused to help. 200 firms failed.

quiz.question: What principle did the Overend Gurney collapse establish?
options: The lender of last resort concept

details.summary: Overend, Gurney & Company was a Victorian-era London bank that collapsed in 1866 after reckless lending to risky ventures. Its failure triggered a financial panic that forced the Bank of England to establish itself as the lender of last resort.
details.whyItMatters: The Overend Gurney crisis defined the modern central banking concept of lender of last resort. The Bank of England's response created principles still used today when central banks intervene during financial panics.
takeaways: Overend Gurney's failure triggered Black Friday on May 11, 1866
The bank had shifted from safe discount activities to risky speculative lending
Walter Bagehot's response formulated the rules for central bank crisis lending

faq.question: What is Bagehot's dictum?
faq.answer: Walter Bagehot wrote that in a crisis, the central bank should lend freely at a penalty rate against good collateral. This principle, born from the Overend Gurney crisis, remains the foundation of how central banks respond to financial panics.

faq.question: How does a Victorian-era bank failure remain relevant today?
faq.answer: The Overend Gurney collapse established that financial systems need a lender of last resort. Every time the Fed or ECB makes emergency loans during a crisis, they are applying principles developed in response to this 1866 bank failure.
